title: Blood Pressure Enzyme’s Hidden Role: Crafting Sulfur Rings to Boost Cellular Antioxidants
body:
A newly discovered function for a well‑known blood‑pressure enzyme could reshape how scientists think about the body’s internal antioxidant defenses. Researchers have found that the enzyme angiotensin‑converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), already famous for its role in regulating blood pressure and as a gateway for the coronavirus, also catalyzes the formation of sulfur‑containing rings that are essential building blocks of a powerful class of cellular antioxidants. The finding opens fresh avenues for therapeutic strategies aimed at neurodegenerative disorders and other conditions linked to oxidative stress.

The study, conducted by a multidisciplinary team of biochemists and neurologists, reveals that ACE2 can convert simple sulfur‑bearing molecules into cyclic thiosulfonates, a type of compound that readily incorporates into glutathione and other endogenous antioxidants. These cyclic structures act as “sulfur rings,” stabilising the antioxidant molecules and enhancing their capacity to neutralise reactive oxygen species (ROS). By performing this previously unknown chemical transformation, ACE2 effectively bolsters the cell’s own defence system against oxidative damage, a process implicated in the onset of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and age‑related cognitive decline.

Historically, ACE2 has been studied primarily for its role in the renin‑angiotensin system, where it counterbalances the vasoconstrictive effects of angiotensin‑II, thereby lowering blood pressure. Its prominence surged during the COVID‑19 pandemic when the virus’s spike protein was shown to bind ACE2, facilitating viral entry into host cells. The new research adds a third, unexpected dimension to the enzyme’s portfolio, suggesting that its physiological importance extends far beyond cardiovascular regulation and viral infection.

The discovery emerged from a series of experiments that combined high‑resolution crystallography with mass‑spectrometry‑based metabolomics. When cultured neuronal cells were supplied with precursor sulfur compounds, the researchers observed a rapid increase in cyclic thiosulfonates, but only in the presence of active ACE2. Inhibiting the enzyme with a specific blocker dramatically reduced the production of these antioxidants, leading to heightened ROS levels and greater cellular damage under oxidative stress. Conversely, overexpressing ACE2 amplified the antioxidant response and protected neurons from toxin‑induced death. These results were corroborated in mouse models, where genetic up‑regulation of ACE2 conferred resistance to chemically induced neurodegeneration.

The implications of these findings are twofold. First, they suggest that pharmacological modulation of ACE2 could become a novel approach to bolster the body’s intrinsic antioxidant capacity, potentially slowing the progression of diseases where oxidative stress is a key driver. Second, the work raises caution for existing ACE2‑targeting drugs, such as certain antihypertensives and experimental COVID‑19 treatments, which might inadvertently diminish this protective antioxidant pathway. “We need to reassess the systemic effects of ACE2 inhibitors and activators,” said Dr. Lina Morales, the study’s senior author. “What was once thought of as a purely vascular target now appears to be a central hub in cellular redox homeostasis.”

Experts not involved in the research have welcomed the discovery but stress that translating it into clinical practice will require careful validation. Dr. Samuel Liu, a neurochemist at the University of Cambridge, noted, “The link between ACE2 activity and sulfur‑ring antioxidant synthesis is compelling, yet we must determine whether enhancing this pathway in humans yields measurable benefits without unintended side effects.” He added that the balance between ACE2’s vasodilatory functions and its newly uncovered antioxidant role may differ across tissues, necessitating targeted delivery methods.

Looking ahead, the research team plans to investigate whether dietary sulfur sources—such as those found in garlic, onions, and cruciferous vegetables—can synergise with ACE2 activity to amplify antioxidant production. Clinical trials are also being designed to test ACE2‑activating compounds in early‑stage Alzheimer’s patients, with the aim of evaluating cognitive outcomes and biomarkers of oxidative stress. If successful, this line of inquiry could usher in a new class of therapeutics that harness the body’s own chemistry to combat neurodegeneration, offering hope for millions worldwide.
